cards.title: How I assess AI readiness: the 0 to 4 method

cards.answer: I score readiness per table, not per organization, because the question is whether people and AI tools can use each table correctly today. Every table gets one level: 0 undocumented, 1 described, 2 usable, 3 governed, 4 AI-ready, and it only reaches a level when it passes every check for that level and those below. Most checks are deterministic, so code scores them the same way every time: description coverage, placeholder or encoding-damage flags, a stated grain, documented keys and join paths, coded columns linked to a lookup, a named owner, usage rules such as validity windows, and for level 4, entry in the semantic layer plus verified questions that pass. Priority is value times gap, with value taken from query logs and dependent reports. The output is a ranked work list per owner. Status: research done, prototype scorer next.

cards.answer: Not until there's a semantic layer under it. These tools are only as accurate as the definitions, joins and verified questions they're given; the vendors' own numbers show it, with Databricks reporting 84.5% against 52.4% and Snowflake about twice the accuracy of a plain model once that layer exists. Most warehouses can't supply it because nobody has written down what each table means in machine-usable form. The pilot I'd run is one subject area, about 50 tables, 4 to 6 weeks: a readiness heatmap, owner work lists, a semantic layer for the top 10 to 15 tables, and 50 verified questions asked against raw tables and then with the layer. That before-and-after accuracy is the deciding number. I'd export through the Open Semantic Interchange where supported, so the layer isn't locked to one platform.

cards.title: Can AI write our missing metadata?
questions: can ai write the missing metadata for our tables

cards.answer: Yes as drafts, never as fact. In my framework AI does two jobs: it extracts rules hidden in prose descriptions into structured fields, and it drafts descriptions for undocumented tables from names, types, comments and lookups. Every draft is labeled AI-inferred, unconfirmed, carries a confidence note, goes to the owner's work list, and changes no score until a person confirms it. The research backs that split: grounded drafts were accepted by data stewards 87 to 88% of the time as is or with minor edits, while fully automatic descriptions recovered only about a third of the text-to-SQL gain human-written ones gave. What the model sees depends on the privacy tier: sample rows for open code tables, profile statistics for internal ones, metadata only for restricted tables, on owned hardware with open-weight models.

cards.answer: Two gates first: real business impact and data that's ready. If either fails, the project doesn't start. After that I rank by value and cost of adoption, not technical interest. On the legislative platform I sequenced the roadmap that way: one intake mailbox covers two of the three most-cited stakeholder pain points, and the only behavior change it asks is adding an address to a CC line. For Sponsored Programs, I prepared a ranked portfolio of nine AI agents across the proposal-to-cash lifecycle, with governance rules: human review, deterministic financial calculations and field-level provenance. I also separate problems that get blurred together, like a payables FAQ chatbot and a procurement price-comparison tool, so effort goes to the right one. And I flag schema decisions that are free now and expensive to retrofit later.

cards.answer: Adopt what's mature, build only the gap, and keep whatever compounds in-house. On the archival pipeline I directed a rubric-scored evaluation of Siegfried, DROID, BitCurator, ExifTool, Apache Tika, Docling, the NSRL set, ePADD, Preservica and Archivematica, with the deliverable being what to adopt, what to skip and what still needed writing. The integration rule: professional tools plug into the pipeline so their updates arrive free, and where the University already holds a license we use it. The readiness research split the same way: data quality monitoring and OpenMetadata coverage metrics are mature, so adopt; the readiness ladder, owner work lists and local-model enrichment don't exist, so build. On the legislative platform, bill data is a commodity any vendor sells, but a model of the institution's own interpretive stance can't be bought.

cards.title: Archival images: vendor moderation API, fine-tuning, or tuning what we have?

cards.answer: I laid it out as a ladder by investment. Cheapest: tune the similarity threshold between 0.35 and 0.55 on a labeled validation set, since semantic similarity already beat LLaVA on historically contextual imagery and LLaVA added latency without accuracy gains. Middle: Google Vision SafeSearch, AWS Rekognition or Azure Content Moderator, the fastest path to reliable nudity and violence detection, with cost and procurement as the constraints. Top: fine-tune LLaVA on labeled University images for domain-specific content such as historical racialized performance and Indigenous cultural materials; most accurate long term, but it needs a labeled training set first. Two things narrowed it later. The production program's privacy position excludes hosted AI services, and 73% of flagged images were ambiguous, so a written appraisal policy and a gold set come before any training.

cards.answer: I build it around a break-even threshold and then try to break it. For the Research Funding platform, 480 AITS hours at $47 an hour came to about $22,560 against a sponsored research base of roughly $1.5 billion a year, so 1x recovery needed a funding uplift of 0.0015%. I checked it against half the adoption, double the hours and a smaller base, and the threshold still sat comfortably below any plausible outcome. Later I re-scoped it to 237 hours across eight roles, under the 250-hour work-request threshold, by reusing the production ingestion pipeline, existing NLP outputs and the validated on-prem inference pattern, without cutting functionality. The workforce case used labor benchmarks: turnover at 50 to 60% of salary, about $269 per vacant workday, giving $155K to $169K a year in benefits, labeled as benchmarks, not guaranteed savings.

cards.title: Making a savings estimate defensible
questions: how do you make a savings estimate defensible
how did you get from $317,583 to $161,564

cards.answer: Compute it from the most defensible matches, in code, normalized per unit. In procurement I matched 42,052 products as identical across four distributors on exact manufacturer plus part number, which is the tier I'd build a business case on. The raw spread looked like $317,583 in savings. Then I found the platform's qsu field, quantity sold as, populated on 6,068,599 of 6,068,888 rows; dividing price by qsu gave true unit prices and removed $156,019, 49.1% of the figure, as pack-size inflation. That left $161,564, which I present as the floor, not the ceiling. The model never does the arithmetic: the LLM's one job is equivalence judgment, returned as JSON, and savings are calculated deterministically in code. The next lever is data, not modeling: prior-year purchase quantities from the two catalog-only distributors could multiply the confirmed figure.

cards.answer: I split by workload shape. On the legislative platform, heavy batch inference runs on institution-owned GPU hardware at no marginal cost, and managed Azure OpenAI with gpt-4o-mini handles low-latency in-app requests, with results cached per bill and prompt so each pair is scored once. For the web tier I wrote a cost and scaling analysis of Basic against Premium v3: the app has a memory-bound ML startup profile, and on Basic it showed a crash loop, semantic search failing under memory pressure and cold-start cache loss, so I recommended the upgrade with the cost laid out. For procurement, the designed production path is App Service B3, the 8 GB floor for the FAISS index, plus Blob Storage and gpt-4o-mini, estimated at about $77 a month. What I haven't measured: GPU purchase cost against a hosted service, and I say so in the document evaluation.

cards.answer: Measure first, and check the serving layer before the card. Our server has one L4 with 23 GB of VRAM and 62 GB of RAM: 7B to 14B models run at full speed, 20B to 30B models fit quantized, and 70B-class is out. I took the position that hardware shouldn't be requested on principle; candidates that fit run a roughly 500-bill test first, since a well-prompted 14B with a strong parser often beats a poorly controlled 70B. The upgrade paths were a second L4, an A100 80GB only if 14B to 30B prove insufficient, or on-demand cloud GPU. The archival images showed why: under Ollama throughput sat flat near 9 images a minute with the GPU at 28 to 31%, so a faster card would have recovered nothing. vLLM on the same L4 reached 55.4 images a minute, a 6.22x speedup.

cards.answer: I write the decision rule before the run: the primary measure, the minimum useful improvement, the interval method, and what a pass earns. The interval's lower bound has to clear the minimum, and a screening win earns a confirmation on fresh cases, not adoption. In the document intelligence evaluation, vote3 was pre-registered as the single confirmatory method before the held-out run, and failed or truncated answers stayed in the denominator as zero. Results came from two machines, so I wrote a conformance contract: SHA-256 fingerprints of the frozen case manifests, every request, the client settings and the scorers, and a merge tool that refuses any export that fails. 40,975 scored rows merged. The outcome was routing per task for the prototype, explicitly not production approval.

cards.answer: Vendor numbers and benchmark scores build a shortlist; the client's own task decides. In my generation screen, the model with the highest IFEval score of the four completed, 0.900, accepted 0 of 20 task groups, while the lowest scorer accepted the most. It cuts the other way too. A deployed Nemotron configuration scored 1 of 12 and 5 of 12 on a contract diagnostic against 5 and 9 for local Qwen3 32B, with truncation at a 600-token budget. I treated that as a configuration question: 192 requests across eight configurations, one mechanism at a time. Budget alone changed nothing; reasoning on at 16,000 tokens lifted it, and on 60 fresh documents strict correctness went from 3 to 13 of 30 on CUAD. That supports enabling reasoning, not a cross-model winner.

cards.answer: Evaluate against the work the platform carries, and plan so nothing is built twice. I've led evaluations and migration planning across KNIME, SAS, IBM Watson and open-source stacks, and I'm moving legacy KNIME workflows to version-controlled Python for reproducibility. When the retirement report was lost with its KNIME environment, the usual argument for staying, preserving working logic, no longer applied, so I went straight to Python. Acceptance was exact reconciliation against past output, but only after checking the HR tables were effective-dated and reconstructable. I froze the spec as a machine-checked contract, 4 files, 21 sheets, 436 columns, validated on every run. For the archival pipeline, Office automation can't run on the Linux GPU server, so porting to Tika and headless LibreOffice became a prerequisite with output parity checked.

cards.title: Prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning: which lever first?
questions: when should we fine tune a model
rag versus fine tuning

is fine tuning worth it for our use case

how would you validate a fine tuned model

cards.answer: Cheapest lever first. Fix the instructions and checks, including contradictions between rules; switch or route models when a candidate passes a pre-registered rule and its confirmation; add retrieval or tools when the gap is missing or changing knowledge; fine-tune only when the best prompt and model still miss the bar and you can produce enough representative examples. In one screen a prompt review found a rule banning the phrase each other while another rule required it, and every model was tested under that conflict. LoRA or QLoRA can make some 27B runs feasible on a 32 GB card, but measure it. The main risk is a model that learns the checks instead of the job, so split before training, hold out cases, and run a regression suite on what the checks can't see.

cards.answer: I ask what in the task actually needs interpretation. Same-shape input and output is a workflow or plain code; ambiguous judgment on fuzzy inputs may need a model. Then I put the model last and narrow. In procurement the instinct is to hand the data to an assistant and ask it to find savings. That fails, because the data quality problem comes first. The design was exact manufacturer and part-number match in under 2 ms, then bge-small embeddings and FAISS narrowing 6 million rows to about 44 candidates in 75 to 110 ms, then qwen2.5:7b judging equivalence on that short list. For an archival appraisal agent, I put agentic loops at folder and collection level, not per file, since an agent loop costs many calls where a classification costs one: hours versus weeks at corpus scale.

cards.answer: When the answer can be computed, compute it. My first accessible chart descriptions used AI; I rebuilt them so every description is calculated by rules from the chart's own data, because AI still gets chart facts wrong, about 1 in 5 numbers in one 2026 study. On the archival pipeline, facts already in a file header are phrased by a model, never discovered by one. In the retirement model I retired the unemployment, DJI and NASDAQ features on structure alone: they vary by time but not by person, so they can't change anyone's rank in a ranking report, and with 21 annual anchors the model can dress a year effect up as a market effect. And about 5% of bills were amendment-heavy outliers over 100,000 tokens; the fix was preprocessing them to the latest changes.

cards.answer: A risk register, a data inventory and controls that live in code. My governance proposals cover resource constraints, long-term support, adoption, LLM output quality, privacy and security, vendor concerns and accessibility, each with a mitigation tied to existing resources. The master data inventory classifies every source by sensitivity, documents every field the AI layer reads, and states the data boundary. On the archival pipeline the position is enforced in code: sensitivity outranks ranking, nothing is deleted, exclusion is a manifest decision, and machine proposals are distinguished from human judgments in an append-only log. On the legislative platform I designed around a specific risk: an AI misstating a named colleague's position inside a FOIA-able system, so users can correct their own characterization before others see it.

cards.answer: Treat them as decision support with layered review, and never let a ranking pose as a probability. Hiring, firing and anything affecting someone's livelihood keep a human accountable. The workforce plan put a fairness check across demographic groups before any individual-level output could be used, with interpretable heuristic fallbacks. On the retirement report, the column labeled probability had never been one: the top bin predicted 42.5% where 5.6% retired. I replaced it with two observed-rate bands, Elevated at 6.3% and Lower at 0.4%, with cut points frozen on earlier years and tested on later ones; a three-band version collapsed prospectively. The output may not be called projected retirements, and whether to rank resemblance or forecast departures is the business's policy choice.

cards.title: Privacy and compliance design: FERPA, HIPAA and PII

cards.answer: Write the data boundary first, then design so the model never sees more than its tier allows. For the Research Funding platform the boundary statement said no new source queries, no extended access, and no document content leaving the on-prem environment for inference. My readiness framework tiers what a model sees: sample rows for open tables, profile statistics for internal ones, metadata only for restricted tables like medical or financial aid, nothing for excluded ones. The image taxonomy maps each category to its basis: FERPA for student records, HIPAA for health records, NAGPRA for human remains. For email, Presidio replaces entities with typed placeholders before a local model summarizes. Local processing is an architectural option; access control, encryption, logging and retention still have to be implemented and verified.

cards.answer: Set the bar before the run, then report against it. For document intelligence the acceptance target for numbers was 99% recall. Every model recovered 96.5% of the numbers in prose crops, and the best table route reached 97.4%, so numeric extraction is review-assisted, not unattended, and the first round recorded that no model or pipeline passed promotion. A small model matching a large one was published next to that gap. Layout masking raised word F1 from 0.814 to 0.881 but cut numeric recall from 0.872 to 0.694, so it stayed experimental. Institutional readiness is gated on a human-labeled set of about 100 documents, 20 double-labeled. For users, I state accuracy as decisions: the bill model is right on about 75% of the bills it flags.

The readiness pilot is one subject area, about 50 tables, 4 to 6 weeks, and passes only if the same 50 verified questions score better with the semantic layer than against raw tables. The workforce proof of concept ran on synthetic data mirroring the warehouse HR tables, so the pipeline was demonstrated before connecting to production data, which is planned under governance review. On the archival build, a written appraisal policy and a 300 to 500 file gold set are prerequisites for triage, and the free-filter reduction rate has to be measured, not assumed. cards.answer: Measure value in use, defined before the build. For bill prediction, AUC wasn't the KPI; I built a validation method around the precision of each call and the days of warning before the floor vote, with safeguards against counting predictions made after the outcome was known. On the held-out 103rd General Assembly that's 75.1% precision and 76.2% recall at a 0.70 threshold, median 21 days' warning. For the Research Funding platform, success meant sponsor approval of the feature schema, validated samples before full-corpus processing, and repeatable scheduled processing after launch. For data readiness, it's verified-question accuracy before and after the semantic layer. On the retirement report I report precision and recall at every candidate threshold, because flag volume is a policy choice.

cards.answer: By phase and role for people, from measured rates for compute, with assumptions marked provisional. The Research Funding plan had hours per activity across four phases, 80, 160, 140 and 100, for 480 hours over three months; the re-scope was 237 hours over about ten weeks, 138 of them development. For compute I time a real sample: the email pipeline measured 347.80 seconds per 10 rows, which projects to about 966 hours for 100,000 messages. I traced the cause, Ollama CLI reloading the model on every call, and listed options with estimates: persistent serving 5 to 10x, parallelism 4 to 8x, cloud APIs 100x or more. The legislative model choice was framed against an 11,673-bill, roughly 155-hour run, so the evaluation was sized to that risk.

cards.answer: Lock the schema with the stakeholder before the build, and never pay for inference to reproduce a column that exists. For the Research Funding platform, every candidate feature was marked already structured, unknown, or not, and whether the LLM should extract it, yes, no or hybrid. Sponsor mapping was deterministic with LLM-assisted matching only for the long tail. On taxonomy I gave three options, anchor on HERDS, an independent LLM taxonomy, or a hybrid, and recommended the hybrid: HERDS as the broad anchor already classifying proposals, LLM themes as finer leaves, reconciled with sentence embeddings. LLM outputs were designed into sibling tables joined on FILE_DATA_ID, with model and prompt version per row. I also put ten candidate data sources on the table at design time, since adding them later costs more.
